topic: Constructive graphwise completeness of latent subpopulation S-ID, including positive finite-binary S-Hedge certificates, compositional inverse lifting through ancestors of S, and an audit of the UK Biobank HbA1c-to-brain-aging application.

open_problems.open_problem: Is Abouei et al.'s latent-variable S-ID Algorithm 1 graphwise complete over finite semi-Markovian augmented ADMGs with strictly positive selected observational laws, with every failure S-Hedge yielding an explicit finite-binary countermodel pair?

source_refs.claim: The paper proves Algorithm 1 sound and explicitly conjectures that failure is also a complete certificate of nonidentifiability.
source_refs.author: Amir Mohammad Abouei, Ehsan Mokhtarian, Negar Kiyavash, Matthias Grossglauser

source_refs.claim: Ordinary semi-Markovian ID has a necessary-and-sufficient graphical criterion whose completeness direction uses hedge countermodels.
source_refs.author: Ilya Shpitser, Judea Pearl

open_problems.why_unsolved: Abouei et al. establish the recursive identifying functional and soundness but leave completeness as a conjecture. Ordinary hedge completeness does not transfer verbatim: S-components may be connected through ancestors of S, and observational equivalence is imposed only on the normalized selected law P(V | S=1). A failure witness must therefore preserve the entire positive selected distribution and its normalization while separating the intervention-before-conditioning target, and then remain valid under the district-factorization lift.
open_problems.what_a_resolution_would_look_like: An iff theorem equating Algorithm 1 success with graphwise identification, plus a terminating success-or-certificate procedure returning the published Eq. 23 functional on success and a symbolic finite-binary SCM pair with common positive P(V | S=1) and distinct P_X(Y | S=1) on failure.

writing_exemplar.why: It is the direct anchor and frames latent-variable S-ID as the missing extension of complete fully observed S-ID.
writing_exemplar.motivation_arc: Subpopulation data differ from population data -> latent confounding invalidates the fully observed S-ID criterion -> S-components and S-Hedges yield a sound recursive algorithm -> determine whether that algorithm exactly characterizes graphwise S-ID.

method_exemplars.technique: Localize recursive ID failure to a hedge, construct two finite recursive semi-Markovian models agreeing observationally and disagreeing interventionally, and lift the witness through c-component factorization.
method_exemplars.why_closest: The desired S-Hedge certificate is the selected-law analogue of the ordinary hedge counterpair used to prove completeness of ID.

method_exemplars.technique: Prove completeness of the Tian-Pearl recursion inductively through strict ancestral and c-component reductions and convert terminal failure into semi-Markovian nonidentifiability.
method_exemplars.why_closest: It provides a second proof architecture for matching recursive failure to a graphwise obstruction while tracking termination by shrinking subgraphs.

method_exemplars.technique: Compile hidden-variable graphical functionals into weight-based and influence-function estimators, with double-robustness and efficiency proofs on suitable ADMG classes.
method_exemplars.why_closest: After Eq. 23 is certified, its district kernels form an observed-law functional for which an explicit estimator and limit-law rung should be derived rather than deferred.

open_problems.open_problem: Can every ordinary hedge counterpair on the projection obtained by suppressing bidirected connectivity internal to Anc(S) be inverse-lifted compositionally through shared or branching ancestors of S while preserving one full positive selected law and target separation?

source_refs.claim: S-components and S-Hedges incorporate ancestors of the selection node, but the paper does not prove a countermodel completeness theorem.
source_refs.author: Amir Mohammad Abouei, Ehsan Mokhtarian, Negar Kiyavash, Matthias Grossglauser

source_refs.claim: SCM conditioning for latent selection preserves causal semantics and interacts well with marginalization and intervention, but it is not an inverse counterpair realization theorem.
source_refs.author: Leihao Chen, Onno Zoeter, Joris M. Mooij

source_refs.excerpt: The attested positive g-identifiability construction ... supplies positive finite same-P(V) separators
exact focal projection lifts them ... while fixing every nonfocal district

open_problems.why_unsolved: The web literature supplies ordinary positive hedge witnesses, latent-selection conditioning, and district factorizations, while the prior CausalSmith runs supply same-P(V) separators and only a single-focal-district lift. None handles several virtual bidirected edges whose realizing ancestor paths overlap or branch inside Anc(S). Edgewise latent assignments then share structural equations and selection normalizers, so independent lifting can alter P(V | S=1) or erase the target contrast. The first missing proof step is a joint coupling lemma, stress-tested on the two-virtual-edge graph B→D→Y, D↔Z1↔B↔Z2↔Y with Z1→S and Z2→S.
open_problems.what_a_resolution_would_look_like: A compositional inverse-lift theorem mapping any positive finite ordinary-hedge pair on the S-component projection to finite-binary semi-Markovian SCMs on the original augmented ADMG with permitted inactive edges, identical strictly positive P(V | S=1), and the same nonzero target separation.

writing_exemplar.why: Its S-component and S-Hedge definitions give the exact notation and proof boundary for stating the missing lift.
writing_exemplar.motivation_arc: Latent S-ID recursion fails on an S-Hedge -> suppressing Anc(S)-internal connectivity exposes ordinary hedge geometry -> ordinary completeness supplies a projected counterpair -> lift that pair through arbitrary shared and branching selection ancestors.

method_exemplars.technique: Use binary parity-style structural countermodels localized to hedge C-forests and then propagate equality and separation through c-component factorization.
method_exemplars.why_closest: These are the donor counterpairs to be lifted; the destination proof must preserve exactly their observational equality and interventional separation.

method_exemplars.technique: Treat selection conditioning as an explicit SCM transformation and use its commutation proofs for conditioning, marginalization, and intervention.
method_exemplars.why_closest: The desired construction reverses an abstraction involving precisely the three operations controlled by that transformation.

method_exemplars.technique: Exploit district and topological factorization to convert graphical functionals into weight-based estimators and derive influence-function limit theory.
method_exemplars.why_closest: If the lift equates the projected and original success regions, the same factorization is the natural interface for an estimator of the lifted Eq. 23 functional.

open_problems.open_problem: Under an explicit augmented ADMG for UK Biobank recruitment, imaging follow-up, medication and disease exclusions, and ancestry restriction, is Tian et al.'s HbA1c-to-brain-age target identifiable from its two selected samples, and which selected-subpopulation estimand does the analysis identify?

source_refs.claim: The study uses nonoverlapping UK Biobank exposure and imaging samples, imposes multiple exclusions, and acknowledges healthy-volunteer and population-structure limitations without an explicit selection graph.
source_refs.author: Cheng Tian, Zhenyao Ye, Rozalina G. McCoy, Yezhi Pan, Chuan Bi, Si Gao, Yizhou Ma, Mo Chen, Jiaao Yu, Tong Lu, L. Elliot Hong, Peter Kochunov, Tianzhou Ma, Shuo Chen, Song Liu

source_refs.claim: Genetic predictors of optional-component participation associate follow-up participation with adiposity, dyslipidemia, education, psychiatric traits, and Alzheimer disease.
source_refs.author: Jessica Tyrrell, Jie Zheng, Robin Beaumont, Kathryn Hinton, Tom G. Richardson, Andrew R. Wood, George Davey Smith, Timothy M. Frayling, Kate Tilling

source_refs.claim: The imaging subsample is healthier than non-imaged UK Biobank participants across cardiometabolic, cognitive, psychological, and lifestyle measures, and selection can attenuate associations.
source_refs.author: Donald M. Lyall, Terry Quinn, Laura M. Lyall, Joey Ward, Jana J. Anderson, Daniel J. Smith, William Stewart, Rona J. Strawbridge, Mark E. S. Bailey, Breda Cullen

source_refs.claim: Probability-weighted UK Biobank analyses show that participation bias can distort SNP effects, genetic correlations, and downstream Mendelian-randomization estimates.
source_refs.author: Tabea Schoeler, Doug Speed, Eleonora Porcu, Nicola Pirastu, Jean-Baptiste Pingault, Zoltan Kutalik

open_problems.why_unsolved: Tian et al.'s relevance, independence, exclusion, and pleiotropy checks do not establish that genetic instruments remain independent of HbA1c-brain-aging confounders after conditioning on recruitment, imaging attendance, medication use, disease history, complete genotype, and ancestry. Empirical studies show those selection events depend on cardiometabolic, neurological, socioeconomic, and genetic traits and can distort MR, yet the analysis neither states an augmented selection graph nor distinguishes P_x(Y | S_imaging=1) from a population effect or a two-context fused target.
open_problems.what_a_resolution_would_look_like: A fully specified selection ADMG and theorem deriving an observed-data functional for the exact HbA1c-to-BAG selected-subpopulation target under auditable assumptions, or an S-Hedge finite-binary pair proving nonidentifiability under only the assumptions the study justifies.

writing_exemplar.why: It supplies the domain-native target, two-sample design, clinical motivation, and exact sample restrictions to audit.
writing_exemplar.motivation_arc: HbA1c is associated with neurodegeneration -> MR is used to seek a causal interpretation -> brain imaging is observed only in a highly selected follow-up subset -> determine which intervention-within-selection target, if any, the two samples identify.

method_exemplars.technique: Apply S-component decomposition and S-Hedge obstruction analysis to P_X(Y | S=1) from a selected observational law.
method_exemplars.why_closest: The application has an intervention target inside an imaging-selected subpopulation with plausible latent common causes of participation and brain aging.

method_exemplars.technique: Use labeled context-selected graphs, latent projections, and district factorization for identification across systematically selected observational regimes.
method_exemplars.why_closest: The study uses two nonoverlapping samples with different measurement regimes, so the selector determines which variables are observed in each dataset.

method_exemplars.technique: Construct influence-function and weight-based estimators for graphically identified hidden-variable effects and establish asymptotic linearity on supported graph classes.
method_exemplars.why_closest: If the audit yields an S-ID functional, this gives a concrete inference route instead of treating estimation from the two selected samples as automatic.

open_problems.open_problem: For finite-binary latent S-ID failures, what is the sharp identified set for P_X(Y | S=1) given a strictly positive selected law, and does it collapse to a singleton exactly when Algorithm 1 succeeds?

source_refs.claim: Algorithm 1 returns an identifying expression or Fail but does not characterize the residual identified set after failure.
source_refs.author: Amir Mohammad Abouei, Ehsan Mokhtarian, Negar Kiyavash, Matthias Grossglauser

source_refs.claim: Discrete causal questions, including models with selection, reduce to polynomial programs yielding sharp or epsilon-sharp bounds.
source_refs.author: Guilherme Duarte, Noam Finkelstein, Dean Knox, Jonathan Mummolo, Ilya Shpitser
source_refs.venue: Journal of the American Statistical Association

open_problems.why_unsolved: Automated response-function bounds must be altered because the fixed input is the normalized conditional law P(V | S=1), not the population joint law including S. The first proof step is to encode selected-law equality with an unknown positive selection normalizer while preserving intervention-before-conditioning semantics. Existing polynomial-bound machinery accommodates selection broadly but does not give an S-Hedge-indexed analytic frontier or prove that universal singleton collapse is equivalent to Algorithm 1 success.
open_problems.what_a_resolution_would_look_like: A finite polynomial-program characterization of the sharp lower and upper endpoints, analytic endpoint formulas on primitive S-Hedges, and a theorem that the interval has zero width for every positive selected law if and only if latent S-ID succeeds.

writing_exemplar.why: It frames partial identification as the principled output when point identification fails and states the computational object explicitly.
writing_exemplar.motivation_arc: Applied causal structures often defeat point identification -> case-specific analytic bounds are brittle -> discrete SCMs admit response-function polynomial programs -> specialize that machinery to selected-law S-Hedges and characterize singleton collapse.

method_exemplars.technique: Enumerate response functions, impose polynomial equality and inequality constraints, and obtain sharp or epsilon-sharp ranges through dual relaxation and spatial branch-and-bound.
method_exemplars.why_closest: The desired object is a sharp range over finite discrete SCMs, with selected-law normalization added to the constraint system.

method_exemplars.technique: Relax estimated constraint sets to form asymptotically valid confidence bounds for optimal values in sample-constrained partial-identification problems.
method_exemplars.why_closest: Sampling uncertainty in P(V | S=1) turns the sharp S-Hedge endpoints into optimization values under estimated constraints.

open_problems.open_problem: For successful latent S-ID functionals produced by Eq. 23, can one derive an efficient influence function and a cross-fitted estimator with a valid root-n limit law under selected-law positivity and latent-ADMG nuisance restrictions?

source_refs.claim: The paper develops graphical identification and a sound algorithm but no semiparametric efficiency theory or inference for Eq. 23.
source_refs.author: Amir Mohammad Abouei, Ehsan Mokhtarian, Negar Kiyavash, Matthias Grossglauser

source_refs.claim: The paper derives weight-based and influence-function estimators for broad ordinary hidden-variable graphical classes because ID outputs are otherwise difficult to estimate.
source_refs.author: Rohit Bhattacharya, Razieh Nabi, Ilya Shpitser

source_refs.claim: One-step and targeted estimators achieve asymptotic linearity and efficiency for treatment-primal-fixable hidden-variable DAGs, but not for selected-law Eq. 23 kernels.
source_refs.author: Anna Guo, Razieh Nabi

open_problems.why_unsolved: Eq. 23 contains selected-law kernels generated by S-component recursion rather than an ordinary ID functional evaluated on an unselected observational distribution. Existing ADMG influence-function results rely on fixing and district factorizations in the ordinary model. The first changed step is the pathwise derivative of kernels normalized by selection, including any equality constraints transmitted through Anc(S); without it, neither the efficient influence function nor the second-order remainder and nuisance-rate conditions are available.
open_problems.what_a_resolution_would_look_like: An explicit efficient influence function for a stated class of Eq. 23 targets, a cross-fitted one-step or targeted estimator, and sufficient nuisance-rate and selected-positivity conditions proving asymptotic linearity, efficiency, and valid confidence intervals.

writing_exemplar.why: Its central motivation is the gap between graphical identification algorithms and usable estimators for their returned functionals.
writing_exemplar.motivation_arc: Hidden-variable graphical identification is mature -> returned functionals are too complex for routine estimation -> fixing and district structure expose influence-function representations -> extend that bridge to Eq. 23 under selected-law sampling.

method_exemplars.technique: Represent latent-ADMG identifying functionals through fixing operators and truncated nested factorization.
method_exemplars.why_closest: A pathwise derivative for Eq. 23 first needs a selected-kernel factorization analogous to the ordinary nested-Markov representation.

method_exemplars.technique: Derive influence functions from primal and dual fixing representations, construct doubly robust estimators, and characterize semiparametric efficiency.
method_exemplars.why_closest: It is the nearest ordinary-ADMG identification-to-inference construction for structurally similar district functionals.

method_exemplars.technique: Use one-step correction and targeted estimation with cross-fitting, a second-order remainder decomposition, and L2 nuisance-rate conditions.
method_exemplars.why_closest: Those proof components transfer once the selected-law efficient influence function and its remainder are derived.

literature_map:
1. Abouei, Mokhtarian, and Kiyavash (AAAI 2024, arXiv:2309.02281) give a sound-and-complete S-ID criterion for fully observed augmented DAGs.
2. Abouei, Mokhtarian, Kiyavash, and Grossglauser (NeurIPS 2024, arXiv:2405.14547) introduce latent S-components and S-Hedges, publish Algorithm 1 and Eq. 23, prove soundness, and explicitly conjecture completeness.
3. Tian and Pearl (AAAI 2002) provide the c-component factorization and general identification recursion that latent S-ID extends.
4. Shpitser and Pearl (AAAI 2006, UCLA R-327) close ordinary semi-Markovian ID with hedge countermodels and c-component lifting.
5. Huang and Valtorta (AMAI 2008, DOI 10.1007/s10472-008-9101-x) independently prove completeness of the Tian-Pearl identification recursion.
6. Richardson, Evans, Robins, and Shpitser (arXiv:1701.06686) formalize latent projection, fixing, and nested-Markov district factorizations.
7. Kivva, Etesami, and Kiyavash (UAI 2023, arXiv:2306.11755) make positivity load-bearing in conditional generalized identification and supply relevant nonidentification model pairs.
8. Bareinboim, Tian, and Pearl (AAAI 2014, DOI 10.1609/aaai.v28i1.9074) give complete recovery conditions under selection bias, but for a different population-recovery target.
9. Bareinboim and Pearl (JCI 2013, DOI 10.1515/jci-2012-0004) use s-hedges for transportability; their selector semantics and data inputs differ from same-selected-law P_X(Y | S=1).
10. Lee, Ghassami, and Shpitser (UAI 2024, arXiv:2404.06602) treat systematic selection into multiple data regimes with context-selected SCMs and labeled latent projections.
11. Chen, Zoeter, and Mooij (arXiv:2401.06925) define SCM conditioning for latent selection and prove compatibility with marginalization and intervention, but not an inverse positive counterpair lift.
12. Bhattacharya, Nabi, and Shpitser (JMLR 2022, arXiv:2003.12659) bridge ordinary hidden-variable identification to weight-based and influence-function estimation; Eq. 23 lacks parallel inference theory.
13. Duarte et al. (JASA 2024, arXiv:2109.13471) turn discrete causal problems including selection into sharp polynomial-program bounds, suggesting a partial-ID continuation after S-ID failure.
14. Tian et al. (Frontiers in Neuroscience 2024, DOI 10.3389/fnins.2023.1335500) use nonoverlapping UK Biobank exposure and imaging samples for HbA1c-to-BAG MR and acknowledge healthy-volunteer and population-structure limits without a selection ADMG.
15. Tyrrell et al. (Nature Communications 2021), Lyall et al. (Brain Communications 2022), and Schoeler et al. (Nature Human Behaviour 2023) show that UK Biobank participation and imaging follow-up are systematically related to cardiometabolic, cognitive, socioeconomic, and genetic traits and can distort MR quantities.
